WEST HDF5 file west.h5), and slice it with the Python slice expression SLICE
(as in [0:2] to select the first two elements of the first axis of the
dataset). The ``slice`` option is most useful for selecting one column (or
more) from a multi-column dataset, such as arises when using a progress
coordinate of multiple dimensions.

Histogram binning
-----------------

By default, histograms are constructed with 100 bins in each dimension. This
can be overridden by specifying -b/--bins, which accepts a number of different
kinds of arguments:

  a single integer N
    N uniformly spaced bins will be used in each dimension.

  a sequence of integers N1,N2,... (comma-separated)
    N1 uniformly spaced bins will be used for the first dimension, N2 for the
    second, and so on.

  a list of lists [[B11, B12, B13,...], [B21, B22, B23,...],...]
    The bin boundaries B11, B12, B13,... will be used for the first dimension,
    B21, B22, B23,... for the second dimension, and so on. These bin
    boundaries need not be uniformly spaced. These expressions will be
    evaluated with Python's ``eval`` construct, with ``np`` available for
    use [e.g. to specify bins using np.arange()].

The first two forms (integer, list of integers) will trigger a scan of all
data in each dimension in order to determine the minimum and maximum values,
which may be very expensive for large datasets. This can be avoided by
explicitly providing bin boundaries using the list-of-lists form.

Note that these bins are *NOT* at all related to the bins used to drive WE
sampling.

Output format
-------------

The output file produced (specified by -o/--output, defaulting to "pdist.h5")
may be fed to plothist to generate plots (or appropriately processed text or
HDF5 files) from this data. In short, the following datasets are created:

  ``histograms``
    Normalized histograms. The first axis corresponds to iteration, and
    remaining axes correspond to dimensions of the input dataset.

  ``/binbounds_0``
    Vector of bin boundaries for the first (index 0) dimension. Additional
    datasets similarly named (/binbounds_1, /binbounds_2,...) are created
    for additional dimensions.

  ``/midpoints_0``
    Vector of bin midpoints for the first (index 0) dimension. Additional
    datasets similarly named are created for additional dimensions.

  ``n_iter``
    Vector of iteration numbers corresponding to the stored histograms (i.e.
    the first axis of the ``histograms`` dataset).

Subsequent processing
---------------------

The output generated by this program (-o/--output, default "pdist.h5") may be
plotted by the ``plothist`` program. See ``plothist --help`` for more
information.

Parallelization
---------------

This tool supports parallelized binning, including reading of input data.
Parallel processing is the default. For simple cases (reading pre-computed
input data, modest numbers of segments), serial processing (--serial) may be
more efficient.

.. option:: -b BINEXPR, --bins BINEXPR

   second dimension, and so on; or a list of lists of boundaries (formatted
   as [[a1, a2,...], [b1, b2,...],... ]), which will use [a1, a2,...] as bin

=====

The ``w_red`` command applies the Reduced Ensemble Dynamics (RED) scheme to estimate steady-state weighted ensemble (WE) fluxes from shorter trajectories. It utilizes data stored in the ``assign.h5`` and ``direct.h5`` files within the analysis directory to perform these calculations.

Usage
-----

.. code-block:: bash

   w_red

Description
-----------

The RED method corrects for the bias introduced by finite simulation times in WE simulations. By analyzing the duration of trajectories between states, it provides more accurate estimates of fluxes through the reaction coordinate.

Configuration
-------------

The ``w_red`` command reads its configuration from the ``west.cfg`` file under the ``west.analysis.red`` section. The following parameters must be specified:

- ``scheme``: Name of the scheme to analyze (e.g., ``DEFAULT``).
- ``istate_label``: Label of the initial state.
- ``fstate_label``: Label of the final state.
- ``nstiter``: Number of steps per iteration.
- ``nstrep``: Number of steps per report interval.

Additionally, the ``west.analysis.kinetics.evolution`` parameter must be set to ``cumulative`` for RED calculations to be supported.

Input Files
-----------

- ``ANALYSIS/<scheme>/direct.h5``: Contains trajectory data including rate evolution information.
- ``ANALYSIS/<scheme>/assign.h5``: Contains population and assignment data.

Output Files
------------

- ``ANALYSIS/<scheme>/direct.h5``: Updated with a new dataset ``red_flux_evolution`` containing the corrected flux values over iterations.

Example Configuration
---------------------

.. code-block:: ini

   [west]
   [west.analysis]
     [west.analysis.red]
       scheme = DEFAULT
       istate_label = A
       fstate_label = B
       nstiter = 1000
       nstrep = 20
     [west.analysis.kinetics]
       evolution = cumulative

Notes
-----

- The RED correction assumes that the system has reached a steady state.
- Only cumulative averaging is currently supported for RED estimates.
- If the ``red_flux_evolution`` dataset already exists in ``direct.h5``, the user will be prompted to overwrite it.

See Also
--------

- :doc:`w_ipa`: For setting up the IPA scheme used by ``w_red``.
- :doc:`w_truncate`: For truncating trajectories in WE simulations.

w_run
=====

The ``w_run`` command is used to start or continue a WEST (Weighted Ensemble Simulation) trajectory. It orchestrates the execution of the simulation by managing the propagation of segments through the weighted ensemble framework, utilizing the configured work manager for parallel execution.

Usage
-----

.. code-block:: bash

   w_run [options]

Options
-------

.. option:: --oneseg

   Only propagate one segment. This is useful for debugging propagators.

.. option:: --help

   Show the help message and exit.

Configuration
-------------

The ``w_run`` command uses the standard WESTPA configuration system. It reads settings from the ``west.cfg`` file and can be overridden using command-line arguments. The following configuration options are relevant:

- ``work_manager``: Specifies the type of work manager to use (e.g., ``thread``, ``mpi``, ``slurm``).
- ``data_manager``: Configures the data storage backend.
- ``system``: Defines the system parameters such as the number of segments and the number of iterations.
- ``propagator``: Specifies the propagator to be used for segment evolution.
- ``we_driver``: Controls the weighted ensemble driver behavior.

The command also supports standard WESTPA arguments via ``westpa.rc.add_args()`` and work manager-specific arguments via ``work_managers.environment.add_wm_args()``.

Execution Flow
--------------

1. **Initialization**:
   - Parses command-line arguments.
   - Processes the configuration using ``westpa.rc.process_args()`` and ``work_managers.environment.process_wm_args()``.
   - Initializes the work manager using ``make_work_manager()``.

2. **Simulation Setup**:
   - Loads the simulation manager, system driver, data manager, WE driver, and propagator.
   - Assigns the system driver to each component for consistency.

3. **Run Execution**:
   - If running on the master process, it:
     - Installs signal handlers for graceful shutdown.
     - Loads plugins.
     - Prepares the run by calling ``sim_manager.prepare_run()``.
     - Begins the simulation loop by calling ``sim_manager.run()``.
     - Finalizes the run by calling ``sim_manager.finalize_run()``.
   - On worker processes, it simply runs the work manager's main loop.

4. **Error Handling**:
   - Catches ``KeyboardInterrupt`` and logs an appropriate message.
   - Catches any other exceptions, logs the error and traceback, and shuts down gracefully.

Example
-------

To start a new WEST simulation:

.. code-block:: bash

   w_run

To debug a single segment:

.. code-block:: bash

   w_run --oneseg

To run with a specific work manager (e.g., MPI):

.. code-block:: bash

   w_run --wm-type mpi
```

w_select
========

The ``w_select`` command selects dynamics segments from a WESTPA simulation based on user-defined criteria. It allows users to specify a predicate function that determines which segments to include in the output. The resulting segments can optionally include their ancestor segments.

.. program:: w_select

Synopsis
--------

::

  w_select [-p MODULE.FUNCTION] [-v] [-a] [-o OUTPUT] [other options]

Description
-----------

The ``w_select`` command identifies segments within specified iterations that match a given predicate function. By default, only the matching segments are stored. If the ``-a`` or ``--include-ancestors`` option is used, the ancestors of matching segments are also included in the output.

The selection process involves:

1. Reading the WESTPA data file.
2. Applying the predicate function to determine matching segments in each iteration.
3. Optionally including ancestor segments of the matches.
4. Writing the results to an output HDF5 file.

Predicate Function
------------------

A predicate function must be provided via the ``-p`` or ``--predicate-function`` option. This function is called as ``predicate(n_iter, iter_group)``, where:

- ``n_iter`` is the iteration number.
- ``iter_group`` is the HDF5 group corresponding to that iteration.

The function should return a collection of segment IDs that match the desired criteria.

To invert the selection, use the ``-v`` or ``--invert`` flag. This causes the tool to select segments that *do not* match the predicate.

Output Format
-------------

The output file (by default ``select.h5``) contains the following datasets:

``/n_iter`` [iteration]
  *(Integer)* Iteration numbers for each entry in other datasets.

``/n_segs`` [iteration]
  *(Integer)* Number of segment IDs matching the predicate (or inverted predicate, if ``-v`` is specified) in the given iteration.

``/seg_ids`` [iteration][segment]
  *(Integer)* Matching segments in each iteration. For an iteration ``n_iter``, only the first ``n_segs[n_iter]`` entries are valid. For example, the full list of matching seg_ids in the first stored iteration is ``seg_ids[0][:n_segs[0]]``.

``/weights`` [iteration][segment]
  *(Floating-point)* Weights for each matching segment in ``/seg_ids``.

Command-Line Arguments
----------------------

.. option:: -p MODULE.FUNCTION, --predicate-function MODULE.FUNCTION

   Use the given predicate function to match segments. This function should take an iteration number and the HDF5 group corresponding to that iteration and return a sequence of segment IDs matching the predicate, as in ``match_predicate(n_iter, iter_group)``.

.. option:: -v, --invert

   Invert the match predicate. Select segments that do not match the predicate instead.

.. option:: -a, --include-ancestors

   Include ancestors of matched segments in the output.

.. option:: -o OUTPUT, --output OUTPUT

   Write output to OUTPUT (default: ``select.h5``).

.. option:: -h, --help

   Show help message and exit.

Example Usage
-------------

To select segments with weights greater than 0.5 in iterations 10 through 20:

.. code-block:: bash

   w_select -p mymodule.my_predicate -o selected_segments.h5 -s 10 -f 20

Where ``mymodule.my_predicate`` is a function defined in ``mymodule.py`` that returns segment IDs matching the criteria.

To include ancestors of selected segments:

.. code-block:: bash

   w_select -p mymodule.my_predicate -a -o selected_with_ancestors.h5

```

----------------

- ``source_field``: Specify a custom database column name.
- ``generated``: Mark the field as database-generated (e.g., auto-incrementing primary keys).
- ``pk``: Mark the field as the primary key.
- ``null``: Allow the field to be NULL in the database.
- ``default``: Set a default value for the field.
- ``unique``: Enforce uniqueness constraint on the field.
- ``index``: Create an index on the field.
- ``description``: Add a description for documentation purposes.

    class EnumField(CharField):

            return value.value

        def to_python_value(self, value: str) -> Enum:
            try:

Model
=====

Models in Tortoise ORM represent database tables and define the structure of your data. Each model corresponds to a table in the database, and each instance of a model represents a row in that table.

Defining a Model
----------------

To define a model, create a class that inherits from ``tortoise.models.Model``. You can specify fields using various field types provided by Tortoise, such as ``IntField``, ``CharField``, etc.

Example::

    from tortoise import models
    from tortoise.fields import IntField, CharField

    class User(models.Model):
        id = IntField(pk=True)
        name = CharField(max_length=50)

Meta Options
------------

You can configure additional options for your model through an inner class named ``Meta``. These options control aspects like table names, indexes, unique constraints, and ordering.

Example::

    class User(models.Model):
        id = IntField(pk=True)
        name = CharField(max_length=50)
        email = CharField(max_length=100)

        class Meta:
            table = "users"
            unique_together = ("name", "email")
            ordering = ["-id"]

Fields
------

Fields define the columns in your database table. Tortoise provides several built-in field types:

- ``IntField`` — Integer field
- ``CharField`` — Character field with maximum length
- ``TextField`` — Text field
- ``BooleanField`` — Boolean field
- ``DateTimeField`` — Date and time field
- ``FloatField`` — Floating point number field
- ``DecimalField`` — Decimal number field
- ``ForeignKeyField`` — Foreign key relationship
- ``OneToOneField`` — One-to-one relationship
- ``ManyToManyField`` — Many-to-many relationship

Example::

    from tortoise.fields import ForeignKeyField, ManyToManyField

    class Author(models.Model):
        id = IntField(pk=True)
        name = CharField(max_length=100)

    class Book(models.Model):
        id = IntField(pk=True)
        title = CharField(max_length=200)
        author = ForeignKeyField("models.Author", related_name="books")
        tags = ManyToManyField("models.Tag", related_name="books")

Relationships
-------------

Tortoise supports different types of relationships between models:

- **Foreign Key**: A many-to-one relationship.
- **One-to-One**: A one-to-one relationship.
- **Many-to-Many**: A many-to-many relationship.

Lazy Relationships
------------------

Tortoise automatically creates lazy properties for foreign key, reverse foreign key, one-to-one, and many-to-many relationships. These properties are accessed on demand and fetched from the database when needed.

Example::

    user = await User.get(id=1)
    print(user.books.all())  # Fetches all books related to this user

Querying Models
---------------

Models support querying via the ``QuerySet`` API. You can filter, order, and retrieve data using methods like ``filter()``, ``order_by()``, ``first()``, ``all()``, etc.

Example::

    users = await User.filter(name__icontains="john").order_by("-id")
    user = await User.get_or_none(email="john@example.com")

Creating and Updating Instances
-------------------------------

Instances of models can be created and updated using the ``save()`` method or by calling ``create()`` directly on the model.

Example::

    user = await User.create(name="John Doe", email="john@example.com")
    user.name = "Jane Doe"
    await user.save()

Deleting Instances
------------------

To delete instances, use the ``delete()`` method on the instance or on a queryset.

Example::

    user = await User.get(id=1)
    await user.delete()

    await User.filter(name__startswith="John").delete()

-------

Tortoise supports signals that allow you to execute code before or after certain operations on models. Available signals include ``pre_save``, ``post_save``, ``pre_delete``, and ``post_delete``.

    from tortoise.signals import pre_save

---------------------

The ``Meta`` class inside a model allows you to configure various aspects of the model's behavior:

- ``table`` — Name of the database table.
- ``app`` — App name associated with the model.
- ``unique_together`` — Tuple of field names that must be unique together.
- ``indexes`` — Indexes to create on the table.
- ``ordering`` — Default ordering for queries.
- ``abstract`` — If ``True``, the model is abstract and won't be created in the database.
- ``table_description`` — Description of the table.

        app = "myapp"
        unique_together = ("username", "email")
        ordering = ["created_at"]
        table_description = "User accounts"

-------------

Models provide several methods for interacting with the database:

- ``save()`` — Save the instance to the database.
- ``delete()`` — Delete the instance from the database.
- ``refresh_from_db()`` — Refresh the instance from the database.
- ``update_from_dict()`` — Update the instance with values from a dictionary.

----------------

Models also expose useful properties:

- ``pk`` — Primary key value of the instance.
- ``_meta`` — Metadata about the model.
- ``_saved_in_db`` — Indicates whether the instance has been saved to the database.

Advanced Usage
--------------

For advanced usage, Tortoise provides features like custom managers, raw SQL queries, transactions, and more. Refer to the respective sections in the documentation for detailed information.

Primary Keys

In Tortoise ORM we require that a model has a primary key.

That primary key will be accessible through a reserved field pk which
will be an alias of whichever field has been nominated as a primary key.
That alias field can be used as a field name when doing filtering e.g.
.filter(pk=...) etc…

Note

We currently support single (non-composite) primary keys of any
indexable field type, but only these field types are recommended:

    IntField
    BigIntField
    CharField
    UUIDField

One must define a primary key by setting a pk parameter to True. If you

A ForeignKeyField is a virtual field, meaning it has no direct DB
backing. Instead it has a field (by default called {FKNAME}_id (that is,
just an _id is appended) that is the actual DB-backing field.

It will just contain the Key value of the related table.

This is an important detail as it would allow one to assign/read the
actual value directly, which could be considered an optimization if the
entire foreign object isn't needed.

Specifying an FK can be done via either passing the object:
